options: The latency of a single instruction
The throughput of a stream of instructions
The clock speed of the processor
The size of the instruction set
questions.explanation: One instruction still takes as long to travel through all the stages - slightly longer, in fact, because of the pipeline registers. What improves is how many instructions finish per second.

questions.prompt: A five-stage pipeline is running with no stalls. How many instructions are in flight at once?
options: One
Two
Five
It depends on the clock speed
questions.explanation: Each stage holds a different instruction, so a full five-stage pipeline has five instructions in progress simultaneously, each at a different point.

questions.prompt: An instruction needs a register that the previous instruction has not written back yet. What kind of hazard is this?
options: Structural hazard
Data hazard
Control hazard
Cache miss
questions.explanation: A data hazard: the data is not ready. Forwarding can often supply the value straight from the ALU output rather than waiting for write-back.

questions.prompt: Why is a branch a problem for a pipeline?
options: Branches take more clock cycles than other instructions
The next instructions are fetched before the branch outcome is known
Branches cannot be decoded in the usual stage
Branches always cause a cache miss
questions.explanation: By the time the branch resolves, the pipeline has already fetched instructions from the wrong path. They must be flushed, and the work is lost. This is a control hazard, and it is why branch prediction matters.

questions.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline has stages taking 2, 3, 2, 4 and 2 ns. What is the fastest clock period the pipeline can run at?
options: 2 ns
2.6 ns
4 ns
13 ns
questions.explanation: Every stage shares one clock, so the period is set by the slowest stage, not by the average and not by the total. The 4 ns stage sets the pace, and the other stages idle for part of each cycle. Balancing stages is therefore as important as adding them.

questions.prompt: Doubling the number of pipeline stages from 5 to 10 will roughly double throughput.
options: True, that is what deeper pipelines are for
False: deeper pipelines raise the branch misprediction penalty and the register overhead
True, provided the clock is unchanged
False, because the instruction set would have to change
questions.explanation: Each extra stage adds a pipeline register with its own delay, so the clock does not scale perfectly. Worse, a mispredicted branch now throws away ten stages of work instead of five. Real designs stopped getting deeper for exactly this reason.
